name: Affine-Transformations Method
text:
# Affine-Transformations Method

Also called: Hybrid method, Image warping method

## Overview
The Affine-Transformations Method is a hybrid volume rendering technique that uses affine transformations to warp volume slices or the entire volume into the image plane so that data samples become pixel-aligned, after which the transformed data is composited to calculate visibility [S1, unofficial]. It is distinct from pure feed-backward ([ray-casting](#6080-ray-casting.md)) methods, which cast rays into the data set, and pure feed-forward (element-tossing) methods, which map data elements directly to the image plane [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The Affine-Transformations Method builds on [Shear-warp](24-shear-warp.md). While [Shear-warp](#24-shear-warp.md) decomposes the view into permutation, shear, and 2D warp components to align rays with slice normals, the broader Affine-Transformations family generalizes this by applying arbitrary affine transformations to warp the volume data (or slices) into a space where they are pixel-aligned with the image plane [S1, unofficial]. Once the data is pixel-aligned, the renderer scans the depth columns to determine pixel color, typically using [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Warp-Space Affine Mixture](4115-warp-space-affine-mixture.md)
[Warp-Space Affine Mixture](#4115-warp-space-affine-mixture.md) is a warping method where affine mixture weights are computed in warped space, outperforming models with no warping, convolutional warps, or world-space mixture. It addresses the limitations of single affine warps and freely-varying template points by using a spatial mixture of affine transformations to produce an inverse warp field, effectively extending linear blend skinning to volumetric space.

### Drebin-Carpenter-Hanrahan Warping
This variant, introduced by Drebin, Carpenter, and Hanrahan in 1988, uses conventional two-pass image warping to resample volume elements in each slice so the resulting slices are pixel-aligned [S1, unofficial]. The renderer then converts the warped data set into multiple data sets: substance, opacity, gradient, and possibly mask [S1, unofficial]. These multiple data sets are used to generate shaded slices, which are composited together to form the final image [S1, unofficial]. Hanrahan later extended this to a three-pass algorithm, developing affine-mapping equations and suggesting that making all magnification passes before minification passes avoids resampling artifacts where information is lost during minification [S1, unofficial].

### World-Space Affine Mixture
A baseline warping variant where the affine mixture is performed in [world space](#2511-voxel-coordinate-systems-and-conversion.md) rather than warped space, meaning mixture weights are not warped before evaluation [S2]. The affine transform is defined as $A_i(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{R}_i(\mathbf{s}_i \circ (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}_i))$ and the normalized mixture weight as $a_i(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{w_i(\mathbf{x})}{\sum_j w_j(\mathbf{x})}$, where $\mathbf{R}_i$ is rotation, $\mathbf{s}_i$ is scale, $\mathbf{t}_i$ is translation, and $w_i$ is the weight volume [S2]. A key pitfall is that since mixture weights are not warped, the decoder must match any motion of the template by moving the mixture weights, which is less efficient [S2].

### Image Transformation Methods
A forward projection method where volume data is transformed so rays can be projected into the volume and onto the image plane using a scan line method at any angle via Euler angle transformations [S3, unofficial]. The transformation is given by $T = P_z Z_e R_z(\phi) R_y(\theta) R_z(\psi)$, where $T$ is the transform, $P$ is the transformation, $R_z$ is perspective z rotation about the Z axis, and $R_y$ is rotation about the y axis [S3, unofficial]. Drebin uses a two-pass image transformation method, while Hanrahan generalized this into a three-pass image transformation method, which is claimed to be more efficient in time and produce higher quality results for general views than Drebin's two-pass technique [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The method originated with Drebin, Carpenter, and Hanrahan in 1988, who presented an earlier Pixar work using feed-forward image warping [S1, unofficial]. Hanrahan extended this in 1990 with a three-pass algorithm [S1, unofficial]. The approach is cited in overviews of volume rendering as a representative hybrid method [S1, unofficial][S3, unofficial].
